c.tagline: High-altitude Andean capital of art, coffee culture and endless nightlife.

taxi.fareNote: Meters run in a unit system (not direct pesos); ask driver or use apps like Cabify/Uber to avoid overcharging, especially from the airport.

emergency.note: 123 is the unified national emergency line reaching police, fire, and medical dispatch in Bogotá.

avoid.reason: Avoid Ciudad Bolívar and the southern peripheries.
Caution in La Candelaria at night and the Santa Fe red-light area; drink-spiking (scopolamine) in nightlife.

hood_desc: Colonial historic core with cobblestone streets, museums (Gold Museum, Botero Museum) and the presidential palace; best for first-time visitors who want to sightsee on foot, though it quiets down and feels less safe at night.
Bogotá's main nightlife and dining hub with the Zona T pedestrian plaza, upscale malls and clubs; suited to travelers who want walkable restaurants, bars and shopping close to their hotel.
Leafy, upscale district with colonial-style plaza, art galleries, craft breweries and fine dining; popular with families and travelers seeking a safer, quieter, more polished base in the north.
Bogotá's largest district, mixing LGBTQ-friendly nightlife (Chapinero Alto/Zona Rosa fringe), universities, and trendy cafes; good value and central for younger travelers and digital nomads.
Bohemian, artsy pocket next to Chapinero known for graffiti, indie boutiques, vintage shops and craft coffee bars; suited to travelers wanting a hip, walkable, mid-priced neighborhood.

Four Seasons Hotel Casa Medina Bogotá

water.note: Tap water in Bogotá's modern, developed areas is treated and safe to drink; older buildings may vary.

transit.hours: TransMilenio operates roughly 4:30am-11:30pm daily; limited night bus service continues after; no 24-hour rail option exists.
transit.note: System is extensive but can be very crowded at rush hour; pickpocketing is a known risk on buses, so keep valuables secure.
transit.pay: Visitors buy or tap a rechargeable Tullave smart card (sold at station kiosks) to enter TransMilenio and SITP buses; cash is not accepted at turnstiles. Cards can be topped up at stations and many convenience stores.

bus: Intercity buses from Terminal de Transporte de Bogotá
train: Turistren heritage tourist train to Zipaquirá (weekends only, not a commuter service)

airport.drive: 20-40 min depending on traffic and destination neighborhood
airport.name: El Dorado International Airport (BOG)

transit.m: Airport shuttle bus to city center (35-50 min)

tip.r: Restaurants often add a voluntary 10% 'propina' line on the bill you can decline; taxis and casual services are not typically tipped.

landmarks: Monserrate
A mountaintop sanctuary reached by cable car or funicular, offering the definitive panoramic photograph of sprawling Bogotá below.
Plaza de Bolívar
The historic heart of the city, ringed by the cathedral, Congress, and City Hall, and the traditional gathering place for pigeons and protests alike.
Gold Museum (Museo del Oro)
Home to the world's largest collection of pre-Hispanic gold artifacts, a dazzling showcase of Colombia's indigenous heritage.
La Candelaria
Bogotá's colonial old town, a maze of colorful houses, balconies, and street art that epitomizes the city's historic character.
Botero Museum
A free museum filled with the signature voluptuous figures of Fernando Botero alongside works by Picasso, Dalí, and Monet.
Catedral Primada de Bogotá
The largest cathedral in Colombia, an imposing neoclassical landmark anchoring the north side of Plaza de Bolívar.
Torre Colpatria
Once Colombia's tallest building, this Art Deco-style skyscraper lights up nightly and offers an observation deck over the city.
Chorro de Quevedo
A charming, legend-shrouded plaza said to be the founding spot of Bogotá, lined with bohemian cafés and street performers.
Simón Bolívar Metropolitan Park
Bogotá's largest urban park, a green escape popular for its lake views, festivals, and photogenic open lawns.
Quinta de Bolívar
The elegant colonial-era estate gifted to Simón Bolívar, set at the foot of Monserrate amid manicured gardens.

train.note: Colombia has no scheduled intercity passenger rail. The only train from Bogotá is the tourist Tren Turístico de la Sabana (turistren.com.co), a heritage weekend service to Zipaquirá and Cajicá — not useful for real long-distance travel, which is done by bus or plane.

bus.note: Long-distance and international coaches leave from the Terminal de Transportes Salitre. Expreso Internacional Ormeño runs the direct international service down the Pacific corridor to Ecuador, Peru and Chile, but it is infrequent — many travelers instead take a domestic bus to Ipiales and change to an Ecuadorian bus at the Rumichaca border. Passport required.

ferry.note: Bogotá sits high in the Andean interior with no ports, so there are no passenger ferries. River and sea boats in Colombia operate from coastal or Amazon towns such as Cartagena, Turbo and Leticia, not the capital.

half.name: Zipaquirá Salt Cathedral

half.name: Laguna de Guatavita
half.blurb: Sacred Muisca crater lake tied to the legend of El Dorado gold.

half.name: Nemocón Salt Mine
half.blurb: Quieter salt mine with striking crystal-lined tunnels and mirror-like brine pools.

half.name: Chingaza National Park
half.blurb: High-altitude páramo wilderness of frailejón plants, lakes and Andean condors.

half.name: La Chorrera Waterfall
half.blurb: Colombia's tallest waterfall, reached by a forested hike through misty mountains.

half.name: Chicaque Natural Park
half.blurb: Private cloud-forest reserve with steep trails, hanging bridges and birdwatching.
